lead: Real filters are specified by a cut-off frequency, a stop-band attenuation and an allowed pass-band ripple. An ideal brick-wall response cannot be built, so we choose a mathematical approximation: Butterworth for a flat pass band, Chebyshev for a sharper transition with ripple. A high-order approximation is split into second-order sections, each with a known Q, and each section is built with one op-amp in a Sallen-Key circuit. The same blocks appear in audio anti-alias filters, ECG front ends and sensor conditioning.
prereq: You need: Chapter 7.1 for the four responses, Unit 3 for Bode plots and roll-off, and Unit 4 for gain margin and the stability limit.

blocks.text: A low-pass filter passes frequencies below ω<sub>c</sub> and attenuates above it. The order n sets the ultimate roll-off at 20n dB per decade. The Butterworth magnitude is |H(jω)|² = 1/(1 + (ω/ω<sub>c</sub>)<sup>2n</sup>). Here ω is the angular frequency in rad/s and ω<sub>c</sub> is the cut-off in rad/s. The response is maximally flat at ω = 0: the first 2n − 1 derivatives of |H|² are zero. There is no pass-band ripple. A second-order Butterworth section has damping ratio ζ = 1/√2 and pole Q = 1/(2ζ) = 0.707.

A fourth-order Butterworth is not four identical sections. It splits into two second-order sections with Q = 0.541 and Q = 1.307. The low-Q section is flat; the high-Q section peaks slightly near f<sub>c</sub>, and the cascade gives the flat Butterworth shape. Some syllabi call d = 1/Q = 2ζ the dissipation factor (some say damping); for Q = 0.707, d = 1.414, twice ζ.

The Chebyshev type-I magnitude is |H(jω)|² = 1/(1 + ε² T<sub>n</sub>²(ω/ω<sub>c</sub>)). T<sub>n</sub> is the Chebyshev polynomial of order n, and ε sets the pass-band ripple. If the allowed ripple is A<sub>p</sub> dB, ε = √(10<sup>A<sub>p</sub>/10</sup> − 1). The response ripples between 1 and 1/√(1 + ε²) in the pass band and then falls faster than Butterworth of the same order. A 1 dB Chebyshev meets a given stop-band specification with a lower order than Butterworth, at the cost of ripple and a poorer phase response. Its section Q values come from tables or a design program.

The equal-component Sallen-Key low-pass uses two equal resistors R and two equal capacitors C. The op-amp is a non-inverting amplifier with gain K = 1 + R<sub>f</sub>/R<sub>1</sub>. R<sub>f</sub> is the feedback resistor from output to inverting input, and R<sub>1</sub> goes from inverting input to ground. The cut-off and pole Q are f<sub>c</sub> = 1/(2πRC) and Q = 1/(3 − K). These hold for K < 3. The second capacitor feeds a fraction of the output back to the RC node; this positive feedback raises Q without an inductor.

For a high-pass response, swap each R with C. The cut-off is still f<sub>c</sub> = 1/(2πRC) and Q = 1/(3 − K). The low-pass to high-pass transformation replaces s/ω<sub>c</sub> by ω<sub>c</sub>/s in the normalized low-pass function, where s is the complex frequency variable. In components, resistors become capacitors and capacitors become resistors, and the gain stage is unchanged.

items: Pick C as a convenient value, usually 1 nF to 100 nF.
Choose R<sub>1</sub> and set R<sub>f</sub> = (K − 1)R<sub>1</sub>. Keep K below 3.

blocks.text: Frequency scaling to a new cut-off f<sub>c</sub>′: divide every capacitor by k or divide every resistor by k, where k = f<sub>c</sub>′/f<sub>c</sub>; f<sub>c</sub> becomes f<sub>c</sub>′ and Q is unchanged. Impedance scaling: multiply every resistor by m and divide every capacitor by m; f<sub>c</sub> and Q stay the same and the impedance level rises by m. To move a designed filter from f<sub>c</sub> to f<sub>c</sub>′, scale all capacitors by f<sub>c</sub>/f<sub>c</sub>′ or scale all resistors by f<sub>c</sub>/f<sub>c</sub>′ (equivalently, divide the resistors by f<sub>c</sub>′/f<sub>c</sub>).

Start with f<sub>c</sub>, the stop-band frequency f<sub>s</sub>, the stop-band attenuation A<sub>s</sub> in dB, and the pass-band ripple A<sub>p</sub> in dB. For Butterworth, the order needed is n ≥ log<sub>10</sub>(10<sup>A<sub>s</sub>/10</sup> − 1) / (2 log<sub>10</sub>(f<sub>s</sub>/f<sub>c</sub>)). Round n up to an integer. For Chebyshev, use the ripple ε and the Chebyshev order formula, or read n from a table. A higher n means more sections and a steeper roll-off.

For an even-order Butterworth, split n into n/2 second-order sections. The Q values are Q<sub>k</sub> = 1/(2 cos((2k − 1)π/(2n))), for k = 1 to n/2. For n = 4, k = 1 gives Q = 0.541 and k = 2 gives Q = 1.307. For odd n, one section is first-order and the rest are second-order. Cascade the sections in any order; put the lowest Q first if you want to avoid internal peaking.

For a high-pass filter, use the same Q values and swap R and C in every section. For a narrow band-pass, apply the low-pass to band-pass transformation s/ω<sub>c</sub> → (s² + ω<sub>0</sub>²)/(B s). Here ω<sub>0</sub> is the centre frequency in rad/s and B is the bandwidth in rad/s. The result has centre ω<sub>0</sub> and quality factor Q<sub>bp</sub> = ω<sub>0</sub>/B. It can be built as a Sallen-Key band-pass or as the single-op-amp positive-feedback circuit some syllabi call Deliyannis-Friend.

spec.aria: A top-to-bottom design flow from filter specifications through order, section Q values and component values to a final Bode plot check.

examples.question: Design a second-order Butterworth low-pass filter with f<sub>c</sub> = 2 kHz using the equal-component Sallen-Key circuit. Take C = 10 nF. Choose standard 1% resistors and R<sub>1</sub> = 10 kΩ. Find R, K and R<sub>f</sub>.
steps: For the equal-component low-pass, R = 1/(2π f<sub>c</sub> C). Substitute f<sub>c</sub> = 2000 Hz and C = 10 × 10<sup>−9</sup> F: R = 1/(2π × 2000 × 10 × 10<sup>−9</sup>) = 7957.7 Ω = 7.96 kΩ. Use the standard 1% value 8.2 kΩ.
A second-order Butterworth has Q = 1/√2 = 0.707. The gain must be K = 3 − 1/Q = 3 − 1.414 = 1.586.
With R<sub>1</sub> = 10 kΩ, R<sub>f</sub> = (K − 1)R<sub>1</sub> = 0.586 × 10 kΩ = 5.86 kΩ. Use the standard 1% value 5.9 kΩ.

The final section uses R = 8.2 kΩ, C = 10 nF, R<sub>1</sub> = 10 kΩ and R<sub>f</sub> = 5.9 kΩ, giving Q ≈ 0.71 and K ≈ 1.59. With R = 8.2 kΩ and C = 10 nF the actual cut-off is 1/(2π × 8.2 kΩ × 10 nF) ≈ 1.94 kHz, about 3% low; use 7.96 kΩ (or trim R) if the 2 kHz value matters.
examples.answer: Use R = 8.2 kΩ, C = 10 nF, K = 1.586 and R<sub>f</sub> = 5.9 kΩ with R<sub>1</sub> = 10 kΩ.
examples.check:
import math
fc = 2000.0
C = 10e-9
R = 1/(2*math.pi*fc*C)
Q = 1/math.sqrt(2)
K = 3 - 1/Q
R1 = 10e3
Rf = (K - 1)*R1
print(round(R/1000, 4))
print(8.2)
print(round(K, 4))
print(round(Rf/1000, 4))
print(5.9)

traps: Taking Q = 1 for a Butterworth section. The second-order Butterworth Q is 0.707; a fourth-order Butterworth needs Q = 0.541 and Q = 1.307.
Forgetting that the Sallen-Key gain must stay below 3. At K = 3, Q becomes infinite and the filter oscillates; above 3 the positive feedback wins.
Using f<sub>c</sub> = 1/(2πRC) when the two resistors or two capacitors are not equal. The simple formula is only for the equal-component circuit.
Confusing pass-band ripple in dB with stop-band attenuation in dB. Chebyshev ripple is allowed inside the pass band; it does not replace the stop-band specification.

Ignoring resistor tolerance. A 5% error in R shifts f<sub>c</sub> by about 5%; Q is set by the gain K = 1 + R<sub>f</sub>/R<sub>1</sub>, so it is mismatch between the two filter resistors or capacitors, and the tolerance of R<sub>f</sub> and R<sub>1</sub>, that changes Q. High-Q sections are the sensitive ones. Use 1% parts for a Q near 1.3.

quiz.q: What is the pole Q of a second-order Butterworth low-pass section?
Why is the Butterworth response called maximally flat?
quiz.a: At ω = 0 the first 2n − 1 derivatives of |H|² are zero, so the pass band is as flat as possible near zero frequency for that order.

quiz.q: An equal-component Sallen-Key low-pass has R = 10 kΩ and C = 10 nF. Find f<sub>c</sub>.
A Sallen-Key section needs Q = 0.707 and has R<sub>1</sub> = 10 kΩ. Find K and R<sub>f</sub>.
A student sets K = 3.1 in an equal-component Sallen-Key low-pass. What happens and why?
quiz.a: Q = 1/(3 − K) = 1/(−0.1) = −10. The negative Q means the positive feedback exceeds the loss, so the circuit is unstable and can oscillate instead of filtering.

quiz.q: A fourth-order Butterworth low-pass uses sections with Q = 0.541 and Q = 1.307. Which section shows more peaking near f<sub>c</sub>, and why?
quiz.a: The Q = 1.307 section peaks more. A higher Q means poles closer to the imaginary axis, so the response rises near f<sub>c</sub> before falling.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of Chebyshev compared with Butterworth of the same order.
quiz.a: Chebyshev has a sharper transition, so it meets a stop-band specification with lower order. It has pass-band ripple and a poorer phase response.

quiz.q: A Butterworth low-pass must give 40 dB attenuation at 4 kHz with f<sub>c</sub> = 2 kHz. Find the minimum order n.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real designs use filter tables and programs such as SciPy or manufacturer tools to get section Qs, then simulate with op-amp gain-bandwidth and slew-rate limits. At high frequencies the Sallen-Key Q depends on the op-amp output resistance and gain-bandwidth product, so a SPICE check is standard. Switched-capacitor filters replace the resistors with clocked capacitors and make the cut-off set by a clock ratio; Chapter 7.3 introduces them. Search next for "Sallen-Key filter design", "Butterworth vs Chebyshev" and "filter section Q".
